Physics-informed neural network for predicting orbital parameters 
of Low Earth Orbit satellites using two line element dataset ✩
Md Sahat Mahmud,

Department of Aeronautical and Aviation Engineering, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, 999077, the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
of China

Received 20 May 2025; received in revised form 3 January 2026; accepted 7 January 2026
Available online 12 January 2026

This research introduces a novel Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) framework using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) archi-
tecture as the baseline model for the precise prediction of orbital parameters of Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites, relying exclusively on pub-
licly available Two-Line Element (TLE) datasets. The proposed method is validated for near-circular orbit with a near zero eccentricity in 
LEO orbits, which is a characteristic of operational LEO constellations such as Iridium, Orbcomm, Starlink, etc. The main goal is to address 
the challenges linked to infrequent updates of TLE data, which generally decreases propagation accuracy with time. The proposed method 
eﬃciently incorporates fundamental physical laws of orbital mechanics into the neural network’s learning framework, improving prediction 
accuracy, stability, and generalizability relative to traditional solely data-driven approaches. Results from the experiments conducted utilizing 
historical TLE records of the IRIDIUM 7 and ORBCOMM FM26 satellites reveal that the integration of physics-based constraints signif-
icantly reduces prediction errors for satellite position and velocity. For IRIDIUM 7 the position and velocity estimates are improved by 87% 
and 70% respectively, which are 50% and 72% respectively for ORBCOMM FM26 satellite. The proposed PINN also demonstrates notable 
improvement over the baseline LSTM, with most R2 improvement for inclination and mean anomaly predictions by approximately 59.5%
and 59.1%, respectively. These improvements are crucial for high-precision applications such as Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT)
as well as space traﬃc management in the increasingly crowded LEO environment, where high ﬁdelity satellite ephemerides are important.

1. Intr oduction

In recent years, the rapid growth of active satellite constel-
lations and the accumulation of orbital debris, particularly in 
Low E arth Orbit (LEO), have raised concerns regarding the
long-term sustainability of Earth’s orbits (Martinez, 2023). 
With the current pace of expansion, the risks of in-orbit col-
lisions and debris proliferation are drastically elevated. How-
ever, the use of outdated or inaccurate orbital data for these

space objects can lead to missed or false collision warnings. 
One prominent example of such issue is the reliance on pub-
licly available Two Line Element (TLE) ﬁles, which remain a 
primary s ource of orbital information for space situational
awareness, but are known to suﬀer from signiﬁcant biases
and errors (Bizalion et al., 2023). To address this challenge, 
the development of high-reliability orbit determination for 
conjunction assessments is an essential prerequisite for eﬀec-
tive space traﬃc management and sustainable operations
(Virgili et al., 2016).

At the same time, LEO mega-constellations such as 
SpaceX’s Starlink and Iridium NEXT have received signiﬁ-
cant interest due to their potential in providing opportunis-
tic Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) services

(Haidar-Ahmad et al., 2022). With thousands of LEO 
satellites now planned or deployed, the dense coverage, 
strong signals these networks oﬀer can be used to augment 
the traditional Global Navigation Satellite Systems 
(GNSS) for navigation services. Researchers hav e begun
exploiting Starlink communication signals for opportunis-
tic PNT, demonstrating meter-level positioning accuracy
using LEO satellites as an alternative to GNSS (Haidar-
Ahmad et al., 2022). Hence, accurate orbit knowledge is 
now crucial for both space-sustainability initiatives and 
advanced LEO based PNT capabilities, making improved
prediction techniques a shared and urgent priority for the
space industry.

Tracking LEO satellites presents a fundamental diﬃ-
culty given the community’s dependence on TLE data for 
orbital parameters. Published by organizations such as 
North 
American 
Aerospace 
Defense 
Command 
(NORAD), TLE sets give each satellite’s publicly accessible 
mean orbital components. These components then can be 
used for orbit propagation with the help of dynamic mod-
els like Simpliﬁed General Perturbations 4 (SGP4). While
convenient and widely used, TLEs suﬀer for limited update
frequency, which eventually degrades the orbit propaga-
tion accuracy over time. In practice, TLE has an update
rate of 1.7 per day (Chen and Lin, 2023) in average, mean-
ing a satellite’s published orbit can be many hours old. 
Using SGP4 to extrapolate the orbit leads to increasing 
errors between updates due to unmodelled forces or 
maneuvers. One study report ed an initial ∼2.5 km orbit
error at the initial epoch increased to over 100 km after
only one week of propagation without new data (Kovar 
et al., 2022). Similarly, initial orbit solution for LEO satel-
lites can be oﬀ by a few kilom eters, with errors compound-
ing until the next TLE update (Haidar-Ahmad et al., 2022). 
This level of inaccuracy is not acceptable for precision and 
sensitive applic ations such as LEO PNT and space traﬃc
management.

To address the constraints of sparse and coarse TLE 
data, numerous orbit determination and prediction 
methodologies have been explored, encompassing conven-
tional numerical propagators that incorporate intricate 
perturbations e.g., Earth’s unevenly distributed gravita-
tional ﬁeld, solar radiation pressure and ﬁltering techniques
e.g., Kalman Filter, Particle Filter, Batch Least Squares
Estimation (Shorten et al., 2025; Levit and Marshall,
2011). Although physics-based models oﬀer high precision, 
they often depend on accurate and regularly updated orbi-
tal parameters, which are generally inaccessible for com-
mercial constellations such as Starlink, Iridium, and
Orbcomm. This limits the practical deployment of such
models for these satellites (Sun et al., 2025). Alternatively, 
machine learning methodologies have been investigated. 
Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM), a type of Recurrent 
Neural Network (RNN), was used to forecast orbital ele-
ments based on prior TLE data (Mahmud et al., 2024). 
Moreover, hybrid approaches that integrate physical 
modelling such as Extended Kalman Filters with neural

networks demonstrated a 90% reduction in ephemeris 
errors 
relative 
to
independent
SGP4
propagation
(Haidar-Ahmad et al.,
2022). Notwithstanding these 
achievements, solely data-driven approaches necessitate 
substantial training data and encounter diﬃculties in gen-
eralizing under ﬂuctuat ing orbital contexts. Recent investi-
gations on amplitude scintillation detection (Li et al., 2024) 
and equatorial plasma bubble modeling (Li and Jiang,
2024) further emphasize the beneﬁts of incorporating 
physics -based insights into data-driven models.

Recently, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) 
have arisen as a formidable alternative, incorporating 
established physics directly into the learning framework. 
PINNs utilize governing orbital equations to limit their 
predictions, necessitating fewer data samples, maintaini ng
physical validity, and demonstrating enhanced robustness,
even under conditions of inadequate historical data or
unclear orbital parameters (Varey et al., 2024). However, 
existing PINN solutions employ static Feed-Forw ard Neu-
ral Networks (FFNN) (Scorsoglio et al., 2023), which do 
not inherently capture the sequential and temporal correla-
tions within historical orbital data. This limits the overall 
prediction accuracy of the existing models limited over 
extended time
horizons.
Additionally,
existing
PINN
approaches often assume availability of high-ﬁdelity and
regularly sampled observational data (Scorsoglio et al.,
2023; Martin and Schaub, 2022), which is scarce for many 
LEO satellites, especially newer ones.

In this work, we propose a PINN based framework, 
with LSTM as the backbone, for improved orbit prediction 
of LEO satellites focusing on the prediction of the six orbi-
tal elements deﬁned by the TLE records: inclination (i), 
right ascension of the ascending node (O, RAAN), eccen-
tricity (e), argument of perigee (x), mean anomaly (M), 
and mean motion (n). The key novelty is the integration 
of LSTM and regularizing the PINN with a customized 
loss function, composed of data loss and physics loss, 
which eﬀectively instructs the neural network to obey the 
physics laws. Additionally, the usage of TLE records as 
training data is advantageous due to their easy accessibility 
and wide coverage. The physics loss is estimated by several 
governing equations, which are diﬀerential equations 
related to the variation of each element. This allows the 
network to leverage the knowledge of orbital mechanics 
(Keplerian motion, perturbation eﬀects, etc.) to ﬁll in the 
gaps between sparse TLE updates. The model was assessed 
on a comparable time span to the typical TLE update inter-
vals and was compared against the baseline LSTM model 
trained with the same data. The outputs were then fed into 
the standard SGP4 propagator to generate the satellite 
state at speciﬁc future epochs for performance evaluation. 
Ultimately, this research introduces a physics-informed 
predictive modeling approach that substantially enhances
orbital parameter estimation accuracy, thereby directly
improving conjunction assessment reliability, orbital debris
mitigation
eﬀectiveness, and
precision
of LEO
PNT
services. By explicitly incorporating physical constraints

into deep learning frameworks, this methodology facilitates 
superior orbital state predictions, advancing operational 
integrity and contri buting to the overarching objective of
sustainable and secure space operations.

2.1. Long short-t erm memory

dependencies in historical data, they often encounter chal-

when gradients diminish signiﬁcantly, restricting the net-
work’s capability to update weights based on distant input
information eﬀectively (Hochreiter et al., 2001). To address 
this problem, LSTMs introduce a special gating mechanism 
which allows them to regulate the ﬂow of information

forget gate – among which the forget gate allows the net-
work to discar d irrelevant past information, input gate
updates the cell state with new relevant data, and the out-

put gate controls what information is passed forward in the 
network. This architecture allows LSTM to retain and 
manipulate

However, raw LSTM networks focus purely on map-
ping the inputs to outputs based on historical data, witho ut
incorporating physical constraints into the network or its
loss function (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997). This 
may result in inaccurate predictions violating the physics 
laws when exposed to new data or conditions. To address 
this problem, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) 
were proposed to incorporate fundamental physica l princi-
ples into the training process directly, ensuring that the pre-

2.2. Physics-informed neural network

PINNs are a class of deep learning models that integrate 
physical laws directly into the neural network ’s learning pro-
cess (Cuomo et al., 2 022). Physical laws are often expressed 
as diﬀerential equations. The diﬀerential governing equations 
serve as constraints or regularizers during training, which 
inherently forces the networks predictions to obey the known 
physics. The method combines machine learning with tradi-
tional computational modeling by including domain knowl-
edge ( such as Newton’s laws or Navier-Stokes equations)
into the model itself (Loshelder et al., 2 025). This approach 
alleviates the concerns of deep learning models being treated 
as ‘Black box’, and provides more trustworthy and transpar-
ent solutions for sensitive systems such as a utonomous driv-
ing, satellite navigation, etc.

PINNs utilize neural networks’ universal approximation 
properties to solve physical system equations (Raissi et al.,
2019). The task of solving diﬀerential equations numeri-
cally transforms into an optimization problem using 
PINNs , which avoids traditional numerical solution meth-
ods (Cuomo et al., 2022). A neural network
with

spatial and temporal information. The loss function

3. PINN governing equations for orbital parameter
prediction

The loss functions of each of the models are modiﬁed 
with the respective governing equations of the orbital ele-
ments. For each of the elements, relevant diﬀerential 
equations-the Keplerian dynamics or Gauss’s Variational 
equations derived from perturbation theory-are incorpo-
rated into the loss to en sure the models consistently obey
the physics laws evolving with perturbative forces and
physical orbital motion. For most of the models, a simpler
approximation of atmospheric drag (Eq. (17)) and J2 eﬀect 
was considered as in the LEO regime, the orbital decay due 
to drag and the perturbative eﬀects of Earth’s J2 are the 
dominant non-Keplerian inﬂuences. For near-circular 
orbits (e ≪ 1, typically e < 0.01 for most operational 
LEO constellations), the periodic and other secular varia-
tions are relatively small and can be well approximated
by the averaged forms used here. The simpliﬁed approach
captures the essential physical behavior without requiring
a full high-ﬁdelity force model, without overcomplicating
the network.

4. Orbital parameter prediction with proposed PINN
4.1. System architect ure

The proposed system architecture is designed to learn 
the temporal evolution of TLE parameters using a PINN, 
constructed on top of a LSTM network. Six separate PINN 
models are proposed, each tailored for estimating one of 
the six orbital elements: n, i, e, X, x, and M. a was not 
modeled explicitly, as it can be deterministically derived 
from n through Kepler’s third law. Excluding it as a 
separate prediction target reduces redundancy and helps 
maintain a lightweight model architecture without compro-
mising completeness. Each PINN model is designed inde-
pendently but operates sequentially to reﬁne predictions
iteratively, resulting in a comprehensive and physically
consistent orbital parameter prediction. The following sub-
sections will discuss the data preprocessing methods and
model training approaches used in the proposed PINN
model.

Although a fully independent parallel architecture might 
appear simpler, the sequential approach is adopted because 
orbital elements exhibit strong physical interdependencies 
(e.g., a is derived from n, both deﬁning orbit size). Sequen-
tial prediction leverages these relationships by using earlier 
predictions as inputs to later models, improving accuracy. 
Additionally, this approach naturally accommodates pro-
gressive feature availability – early models use only basic
features (T, Ds, Dm), while later models beneﬁt from previ-
ously predicted elements.
4.1.1. Data pre-p rocessing

Prior to training the model, raw TLE data needs to go 
through a preprocessing pipeline designed to enhance data 
suitability for training purposes. Raw TLE consists of out-
liers, spikes and ﬂuctuations, which may degrade the per-
formance of the model. The preprocessing pipeline ﬁrst
extracts the relevant orbital parameters and ﬁlters out the
outliers. Other preprocessing steps include:

(1) Converting the raw O to sin O as sud den ﬂuctuations
may cause discontinuity,
(2) Converting the i to sin i,
(3) Calculating and appending the values of Earth-to-
Sun distance (Ds) and Earth-to-Moon distance (Dm)
in the TLE data frame,
(4) Calculating and appending semi-major axis (a) and 
true anomaly (v) into the data frame using the basic

(5) Normalizing the training dataset since the orbital ele-
ments are all measured in diﬀerent scales.

train the PINN: Epoch data in raw format (T), O, n, M, 
e, x, i, Ds,  Dm, a and v. The periodic variation of Ds and 
Dm has resulted in the incorporation of these distances as 
training features for the LSTM model at each TLE epoc h.
RNNs frequently improve by incorporating additional per-
tinent features, as these features facilitate the models in
comprehending intricate relationships and interactions
among many aspects inﬂuencing satellite orbits. Signiﬁcant
enhancement in the model was observed with the utiliza-
tion of these two elements (Mahmud et al., 2024).

For predicting each of the orbital elements, six diﬀerent 
PINN models were employed as shown in Fig. 3. Each of 
the models has a unique customized loss function built with
their respective governing equations discussed in Sec-
tion 4.1. The PINN model is structured around an LSTM 
neural network optimized speciﬁcally for sequenti al predic-
tion tasks. The LSTM network architecture is composed of

interconnected gating mechanism, which enables the model 
to capture long-term dependencies and mitigate the vanish-
ing gradient problem inherent in standard RNN. For all six 
models, the input data is segmented into ﬁxed length 
sequences of 50-time steps, corresponding to most recent 
50 epochs. This segmentation is important to capture the 
temporal patterns in the orbital data. The length of the
sequence was empirically selected to balance both temporal
coverage and computational eﬃciency, making sure that
the network acquires adequate historical data to generate
precise predictions without incurring signiﬁcant memory
expenses or gradient degradation.

6. Conclusion and futu re work

This paper introduces a novel PINN based on LSTM 
framework that delivers quantitative improvements far 
beyond traditional TLE propagation. Speciﬁcally, for the 
IRIDIUM 7 satellite, the position and velocity RMSEs 
were reduced by 87% from ∼650 m to ∼85 m and 70% from 
∼0.65 m/s to ∼0.2 m/s, respectively, while for ORBCOMM 
FM26 the RMSEs were reduced by 50% from ∼1360 m to 
∼680 m and 72% from ∼1.35 m/s to ∼0.3 m/s, respectively. 
The proposed model has also demonstrated signiﬁcant 
improvement over the baseline LSTM, achieving notable 
R2 score enhancements, particularly for i, with an improve-
ment of approximately 59.5%, and M, with an enhance-
ment of approximately 59.1%. These improvements are 
achieved using only publicly available, sparsely updated 
TLE dataset, which clearly indicates that embedding rele-
vant physical constraints into the network’s loss function 
yields signiﬁcant accuracy and more stable predictions. 
Furthermore, experiments conducted on seven additional 
Iridium satellites evaluated the robustness and generaliza-
tion capabilities of the model. The percentage MAE 
improvements of each of the six orbital elements revealed
that careful ﬁne-tuning of the physics loss weighting consis-
tently yielded substantial performance gains across diverse
orbital conditions. Although optimal weight values varied
slightly among satellites and orbital elements, these results
underscore the critical importance and eﬃcacy of physics
weight selection. Moreover, the proposed framework is
seen to be consistently outperforming a purely data-
driven LSTM baseline model across all six orbital elements
predictions – even when trained with a smaller dataset – by
mitigating high-frequency noise and eliminating wrap-
around discontinuities at 0-360° boundaries. Overall, these
ﬁndings validate that the proposed PINN framework not
only outperforms traditional propagation techniques but

also ensures robust, accurate and reliable orbit pred iction
over multi orbit horizons.

Despite signiﬁcant advancements, there exist several 
areas for future research. Primarily, future developments 
should aim at enhancing the current PINN framework 
for higher eccentricity LEO orbits by incorporating more 
comprehensive and higher-ﬁdelity physical modeling, such 
as detailed atmospheric drag models (e.g., Jacchia-Roberts 
and NRLMSISE) and advanced gravitational ﬁeld models 
extending beyond the J2 perturbation approximation. Inte-
grating additional perturbative eﬀects, including solar radi-
ation pressure and third-body gravitational inﬂuences,
would likely improve model accuracy, particularly for
extended forecasting horizons. Additionally, other deep
learning models as base model and feature engineering
can be explored to mitigate the problem of wrap-around
discontinuity.

In conclusion, continued reﬁnement and thorough vali-
dation of the proposed PINN framework are expected to 
signiﬁcantly improve the operational reliability of satellite 
systems, leadi ng to enhanced space sustainability and eﬀec-
tive
management
